content_metadata.description: "A History of Violence" follows Tom Stall, a seemingly ordinary family man who is forced to confront his dark past as a hitman when his past life resurfaces, threatening his family and the peaceful existence he's built. As secrets unravel and violence erupts, Tom's dual identity raises questions about the nature of violence and the possibility of redemption.

qAndA.answer: The large scar over Fogarty's left eye acts as a constant reminder of his violent past and serves as a visual representation of the lasting impact of violence.
qAndA.question: What object symbolizes Fogarty's violent past?

qAndA.answer: Initially, Jack is shocked and fearful, but as the film progresses, he starts to exhibit similar violent tendencies, suggesting a cyclical nature of violence.
qAndA.question: How does Tom's son, Jack, react when he witnesses his father's violent abilities?

qAndA.answer: The reference to Cronenberg's "The Fly" subtly foreshadows the transformation Tom undergoes as he's forced to embrace his violent past. It also connects to Cronenberg's wider thematic exploration of identity and body horror.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the "The Fly" reference in Scene 4?

qAndA.answer: The film deconstructs the idealized image of the American hero by revealing the dark past of its protagonist. Tom's capacity for violence, while initially presented as heroic, becomes increasingly disturbing as his true nature emerges.
qAndA.question: How does the film challenge conventional views of heroism?

qAndA.answer: The ending is unsettling and ambiguous. While Tom returns to his family, the violence he has experienced and inflicted leaves a lasting impact. The final shot of Tom looking distressed suggests that his violent past will continue to haunt him and his family.
qAndA.question: What is the overall mood of the film's ending?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: A film in three minutes, a history of violence. What is violence to you? Is it something that should
be avoided at all times? Can it ever be used for good? Or is it simply a natural state of being,
and inescapable byproduct of our evolutionary existence, that defines us more than we could ever want
to realise? Because in David Cronenberg's 2005 drama A History of Violence, an ordinary all-American
family is about to find out what the consequences of one individual's violent past will mean for them.
Loosely based on the graphic novel penned by John Wagner, the story is set in the fictional
town of Milbrooke, Indiana, and follows the life of Diner owner Tom Storl, played by Vigor Mortensen.
Storl leads the perfect life of his family in the sleepy town until one night two spree killers
attempt to rob and murder him in his patrons, with both men meeting a grisly end thanks to Tom's heroic
efforts. Leading him to being portrayed as a local hero on the news, that catches the eye of a
mysterious gangster named Fogathe, played by Ed Harris. Fogathe arrives in town and publicly
challenges Tom's identity, claiming that he is actually a professional hitman named Joey
from Philadelphia, causing Tom's family to question not only his identity, but also what he is
capable of. Diverting from his usual trademark themes revolving around body horror and science
fiction, director Cronenberg this time focuses purely on the exploration of character. The
superficially simplistic plot acts merely as a wire framework for us the audience to explore
the conflicting psychologies of Tom and his family as his violent past is gradually revealed to us.
We are forced to ask, can a human being ever be the same once exposed to violence,
or is the violence they commit merely a way of preserving who they think they are?
Do we view people differently when we know they have a violent past out of fear for what they
might do to us, or simply for the fact that they ever had the ability to be violent at all?
It's these questions and more that make the film stand out from seemingly similar dramas,
as Cronenberg's direction forces us sometimes at point blank range and with great brutality
to consider not just the act of violence portrayed on screen, but to what the cognitive
effects such events will have on a person and a community for years to come.
Vigo Mortensen plays Tom with a quiet, subdued energy and appears as genial as he does
restrained, but Ed Harris's disturbing performance as Foggy-T is the real scene-stealer,
with his menacing scarred eye acting as a physical reminder of how we all wear violence from our past
differently. The story's ferocity, both visual and implied, acts as its own message on how violence
reveals to us our inner natures and can sometimes enable us to discover things about ourselves,
we never knew or wanted to know we possessed. Leaving us all to ask whether any moralistic
questions on violence really even matter when survival of its most basic kind is at stake.
A question that's Tom and also perhaps one day ourselves will have to answer whether we want to or not.
